Method: Adaptive high-fidelity numerical propagation with mission-specific force-model selection
Accuracy Ceiling: Highest practical ceiling when the force model, tolerances, and data inputs are appropriate; the Molniya case study explicitly tunes retained geopotential degree and integrator tolerance to a prescribed positional-accuracy requirement. [1]
Runtime: Slowest of the main options, but can be substantially reduced by dropping perturbations whose effects are below the mission error budget and adapting geopotential degree with altitude. [1]
Heo Suitability: Best overall for operational-quality ephemerides, orbit determination, maneuver analysis, and final mission validation. [1]
Best Use: Final design closure, OD, covariance and maneuver analysis, collision or conjunction work, and high-consequence operations. [1]
Main Tradeoff: Computational cost and sensitivity to force-model, event-handling, and numerical-tolerance choices. [1, 2]

Method: Regularized numerical propagation: Sundman, KS, or related transformations
Accuracy Ceiling: Very high for strongly eccentric motion because the independent variable allocates smaller effective steps near perigee; KS scaling can maintain the Kepler-energy relation with negligible extra cost in the reported formulation. [3, 4]
Runtime: Usually faster or more stable than an unregularized formulation at the same target accuracy, especially when perigee dynamics dominate; the exact advantage depends on perturbations and implementation. [3]
Heo Suitability: Excellent for extreme eccentricity, close-perigee passages, long integrations, and research-grade propagator development. [3, 4]
Best Use: High-eccentricity orbit integration, perturbed two-body problems, and cases where conventional Cartesian or element propagation becomes inefficient. [3, 4]
Main Tradeoff: Event termination and timing reconstruction can introduce phasing errors; geometric accuracy alone can overstate end-to-end accuracy. [2]

Accuracy Ceiling: High for long-term secular and periodic behavior when the averaged model matches the orbit regime; HEO-specific implementations include major gravitational and nongravitational effects for GTO and Molniya-type orbits. [5]
Runtime: Typically faster than repeated high-fidelity numerical integration over long arcs because it propagates mean elements; the HEO-specific implementation is explicitly designed for long-term propagation. [5]
Heo Suitability: Best speed–fidelity compromise for long-term HEO evolution, preliminary design, station-keeping studies, and large parameter sweeps.
Best Use: Long-arc orbit evolution, constellation trade studies, stability screening, and mission design where rapid repeated propagation matters.
Main Tradeoff: Short-period, event-time, maneuver, and strongly non-averaged effects may require numerical refinement or correction. [5, 2]

Accuracy Ceiling: Very high for the idealized two-body portion of the problem, but limited for real HEO operations unless perturbations and maneuvers are added through separate models.
Runtime: Fastest baseline option and useful inside trajectory optimization, Lambert solvers, initial-guess generation, and large design-space searches.
Heo Suitability: Excellent for preliminary trajectory design and embedded inner-loop calculations; insufficient alone for final HEO ephemerides.
Best Use: Fast screening, transfer design, initial conditions, and unperturbed or weakly perturbed segments.
Main Tradeoff: The speed comes from omitting or simplifying perturbations; accuracy can degrade over long arcs or around maneuver and event boundaries.

Accuracy Ceiling: Potentially high when it switches models according to the mission error budget; the Molniya study demonstrates this principle by matching force-model complexity to required positional accuracy. [1]
Runtime: Potentially near semi-analytical speed for benign portions of the arc while retaining numerical fidelity where needed; performance is implementation-dependent.
Heo Suitability: Very good for operational systems that need scalable propagation across many HEO scenarios, but requires careful validation at model-switch boundaries.
Best Use: Constellations, Monte Carlo analysis, onboard or near-real-time applications, and mixed-fidelity mission pipelines.
Main Tradeoff: Complexity of validation, consistency between models, and possible discontinuities or hidden error when switching fidelity.

Method: Generic fixed-step or non-specialized high-order integrators
Accuracy Ceiling: Can be accurate with sufficiently small steps and tight tolerances, but does not inherently account for the extreme time-scale variation between perigee and apogee.
Runtime: Often inefficient for HEO because a step size safe at perigee wastes computation near apogee; specialized transformations were developed specifically to address this imbalance. [3]
Heo Suitability: Acceptable for short arcs, prototyping, or moderate eccentricity; generally not the preferred production method for extreme HEO without adaptive control or regularization.
Best Use: Baseline comparison, simple simulations, and validation against more specialized methods.
Main Tradeoff: Poorer accuracy-per-compute ratio and greater risk of perigee under-resolution or excessive apogee oversampling.
